title: Fewest Rooms for All Meetings
statement:
You get a day's meetings, meetings[i] = [start, end] with start < end, in no particular order. Each meeting needs a room to itself for its whole length. Return the smallest number of rooms that can hold all of them.

Meetings are half-open: a meeting runs from start up to, but not including, end. So [1, 5] and [5, 8] do not overlap, and the second can use the room the first just left.

examples.why: [2, 7] overlaps two meetings, but those two do not overlap each other: the room [3, 5] used is free again by 6. At no moment are more than two meetings running.
Each meeting starts exactly when the previous one ends, so one room is reused all day.
At time 3 the first three meetings are all running.

hints: The answer is the largest number of meetings running at the same moment. Counting, for each meeting, how many others it overlaps gives too much (example 1).
Go through meetings in order of start time. When a meeting starts, is any room already free? You only need to know the earliest end among the rooms in use.

Keep a min-heap of end times for rooms in use. For each meeting in start order, if the earliest end is ≤ its start, reuse that room (pop). Push its end. The heap's largest size is the answer. Or sort starts and ends separately and sweep.

explain.intuition:
The number of rooms you need is the largest number of meetings running at the same moment. You cannot do with fewer, and a careful assignment never needs more. To find that peak, replay the day in start order and keep track of the rooms in use.

When a meeting starts, the only room that matters is the one that frees up soonest. If it is already free (its meeting ended at or before this start), reuse it; otherwise open a new room. A min-heap of end times gives you the soonest end in O(log n). The heap holds one entry per room in use, so its largest size is the answer.

A slicker version drops the pairing: sort all starts and all ends separately. Walk the starts; each start either reuses a room because the earliest unused end is ≤ it, or needs a new one. Because meetings are half-open, an end at time 5 frees the room for a start at 5, so ends are checked with ≤.
steps: For each meeting [s, e]: if the heap's smallest end is ≤ s, pop it: that room is free again.
Push e: this meeting now occupies a room.
Track the largest heap size; return it (0 for no meetings).
pitfalls: Counting, for one meeting, all meetings that overlap it. In example 1 that gives 3 for [2, 7], but [3, 5] and [6, 9] never run at the same time.
Treating touching meetings as overlapping. With < instead of ≤, example 2 needs 3 rooms instead of 1.
Processing meetings in input order. A room freed early must be reused by a later-starting meeting, so the sweep has to follow time order.

solutions.title: Count at every start
solutions.idea: The peak always happens at some meeting's start. For each start time, count the meetings running at that instant.

solutions.title: Min-heap of end times
solutions.idea: In start order, reuse the room that frees up soonest if it is free; otherwise open a new one. The heap holds the end time of each room in use.

solutions.title: Sorted starts and ends
solutions.idea: Sort start times and end times separately. Each start either reuses a room, because the earliest end not yet used is at or before it, or needs a new room.

followups: Return which room each meeting goes to, not just the count. Which solution makes that easy?
Rooms have different sizes and meetings have different head counts. Does the greedy still work?
